A black stone is found in the Nile similar to a bean, and upon seeing it, dogs do not bark. You might also carry a dog's tongue placed under the big toe in your shoe; or if you carry a dried dog's heart with you, according to <term>Sextus</term> <note>Sextus Placitus, a 4th-century medical writer</note>. Or carry a hare's hair or dung, according to Pliny. Or you might carry the severed tail of a young weasel on your foot, or give the dog a toad in a morsel of food; all these things serve to avoid the barking of dogs. <term>Nigidius</term> <note>Publius Nigidius Figulus, a Roman scholar and contemporary of Cicero</note> says that dogs flee the sight of anyone for an entire day who removes a tick from a pig and carries it about for a little while. <term>Oppianus</term> <note>A 2nd-century Greco-Roman poet who wrote on hunting and fishing</note> writes:

> If you should carry even a small piece cut from the skin of a hyena,
> Immediately the pups and fierce dogs will be struck
> With a bitter terror, nor hereafter will they bark at you
> As you walk by, even if they had barked before.

### How a dog may be unable to run.

If you smear its paws with oil, it will be hindered in its running; it happens in this manner.

### How a hawk may be made courageous.

You shall encourage the bird against the prey so that it attacks large birds. Moisten the food which it uses during the time of hunting with wine; or if it is a goshawk, give it a little vinegar. When you wish it to fly, give it three morsels of meat moistened with wine, or pour wine from a flask into the beak of a young pigeon and then let the hawk fly. In this way:

### You shall make partridges more pugnacious,

If you give them branches of <term>adiantum</term> <gloss>maidenhair fern</gloss> in their food, according to Pliny. Also:

### Roosters are made more pugnacious,

By giving them garlic in their food just before they are about to fight; for which reason, most wittily in the Old Comedy <note>Ancient Greek comedy, specifically referring to Aristophanes</note>, the term <term>eskorodismenoi</term> <gloss>those who have been fed garlic</gloss> was used for those who were vehement and too inclined toward a fight.

### Lest a bird fly high,

Pluck out the tail feathers which direct the course upward; thus it will fly in a circle below. If you wish:

### That a bird cannot fly,

Cut the upper and lower sinews of the wing, and it remains without harm; the bird will not fly, and in this manner they do not escape from aviaries.

<summary>This page provides folklore and practical methods for animal control, including charms to silence dogs, techniques to embolden hawks and roosters for hunting or fighting, and ways to prevent birds from escaping.</summary>
<keywords>animal husbandry, hunting lore, dogs, hawks, partridges, falconry, folk medicine, ancient authorities</keywords>

shines through piety, religion, prudence, and the worship and veneration of God. This is perceived as if by the eyes through true reason, and the confidence of his belief makes him stand out among men as much as the sun outshines the other stars with its light. For the sun itself illuminates the other stars not so much by the magnitude of its power as by its divinity and holiness. Believe that this sun, O Asclepius, is second only to God, governing all other things and illuminating all worldly creatures, whether they are animate or inanimate. 

For if the world <note>original: "mundus"</note> is a living being <note>original: "animal"</note> that lives forever, and has been, and is, and shall be, nothing in the world is mortal. Since every single part of a living being exists within the world itself as if in one and the same eternally living animal, there is no place for mortality. Therefore, God must be most full of life and eternity itself, if it is necessary for him to live forever. 

The sun, therefore, just like the world, is everlasting; thus he himself is always the governor of vital things, or rather the guardian and dispenser of their entire livelihood. God is the eternal governor of all living things, or of the life-forces that are in the world, and the eternal dispenser of life itself. He dispensed this once by an eternal law, providing life to all living things in this manner, which I shall now describe.

<summary>Hermes explains that the pious man shines like the sun, which is the second god and governor of all life. He argues that since the world is an eternally living being, nothing within it truly dies, and the sun acts as the eternal dispenser of life.</summary>
<keywords>piety, sun, cosmic hierarchy, eternal life, living world, Asclepius, divine governance, immortality</keywords>

Marcus Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar and writer</note> testifies that he saw these things. And there are even more wonderful things than these: for on the Attic shore, the sea sounds like a lute. At Megara <note>A Greek city-state</note>, a certain rock rings out like a lyre when struck by pebbles, so great is the power of Music. It <unclear>e</unclear>ven <note>Original: "quidem"</note> soothes the soul, lifts the mind, incites warriors to <unclear>war</unclear> <note>Original: "bellum"</note>, and <unclear>re</unclear>lieves the labor and fatigue of individual works. It recalls those who have fallen and are in despair, and comforts travelers. And the Arabs say that camels carrying burdens are comforted by their singing drivers. In a similar way, those carrying heavy loads sing, and are made more capable and relieved by it: for song produces delight and capability; it mitigates the wrathful, cheers the sad and anxious, pacifies those in discord, tempers the madness of the frantic, and dissipates vain thoughts. From this it follows that Democritus and Theophrastus <note>Successor to Aristotle</note> affirm that some diseases of the body and mind can be either cured or induced in this way. Thus we read that Terpander and Arion of Methymna <note>Greek poets and musicians</note>...

<summary>This page discusses the marvelous and therapeutic effects of music, citing examples from nature, such as the singing shores of Megara, and its ability to relieve labor and heal psychological distress.</summary>

<meta>continues from previous page: for envy has departed from us;</meta> indeed, the Good is innate to Truth, together with life and light, and no avenger has approached further. Truly, all avengers <note>original: "ultrices"; the twelve vices or punishing forces previously mentioned</note> have been cast out by a certain sudden impulse. 

You have understood, my son, the manner of this rebirth. Since the **number ten** <note>original: "denario numero"; the decad, representing a perfect or divine completion</note> is present, the intellectual generation is composed, which rejects the **number twelve** <note>original: "duodenariū numerū"; the dodecad, associated here with the zodiacal vices</note>. We have observed this from the generation itself. Therefore, whoever loses physical sensation for the sake of the benevolence of the generation which is according to God, knows himself to be composed of divine elements. Having become unswerving, he rejoices in divine power with his whole mind.

**TATIUS.** O father, I conceive this not by the sight of my eyes, but by the action of the mind, which is exercised through inner powers. I am in heaven; I am in the earth; in the water; in the air. I am in animals; in trees; in the body; before the body; and after the body. But I wish you would tell me this besides: how the avenging darknesses, twelve in number, are repelled by the ten powers? By what method, Trismegistus?

**HERMES.** This tabernacle, O son, is constituted from the **zodiac circle** <note>original: "zodiaco circulo"</note>, which consists of that number twelve. The numbers are eleven; there is one that is all-formed according to the ideas of nature, for the wandering and circuit of man. Therefore, those avengers are in a certain way separated from one another, yet in action they are in some way joined together. For behold, recklessness is inseparable from wrath. Rightly then, according to correct reason, there is an interval insofar as they are repelled by the ten powers, that is, by the number ten. The number ten, O son, is the generator of the soul. Indeed, Life

<summary>Hermes explains how the ten divine powers or virtues expel the twelve zodiacal vices to complete the spiritual rebirth of the soul. Tatius describes a state of cosmic consciousness where he feels present in all elements and beings.</summary>
<keywords>rebirth, decad, dodecad, zodiac, cosmic consciousness, Hermes Trismegistus, Tatius, divine powers</keywords>

and it will mix itself with the waters of its own fountain. Therefore, the <term>intelligible</term> <gloss>perceived by the mind</gloss> gods are the princes of all species. These are followed by the gods whose prince is <term>ousia</term> <gloss>essence or substance</gloss>. These are the <term>sensible</term> <gloss>perceived by the senses</gloss> gods, similar to their dual origin, who produce all things through a sensible nature, each one illuminating his own work through the other.

Of the heaven, or whatever is understood by that name, the <term>ousiarches</term> <gloss>ruler of essence</gloss> is **Jupiter** <margin>Jupiter</margin>. For through the heaven, Jupiter provides life to all things.

Of the sun, the <term>ousiarches</term> <gloss>ruler of essence</gloss> is **Light** <margin>Light</margin>. For the Good of light is poured into us through the orb of the sun.

The thirty-six <note>Referring to the thirty-six decans of the zodiac.</note>, whose name is the **Horoscopes** <margin>Horoscopes</margin>, are the stars always fixed in the same place. Their <term>ousiarches</term> <gloss>ruler of essence</gloss> or prince is the one they call **Pantomorphos** <margin>Pantomorphos</margin> or the **Omniform** <note>original: "Omniformem", meaning "having all forms."</note>, who creates different forms from different species.

The seven spheres that are called "wandering" <note>The seven classical planets.</note> have their <term>ousiarchas</term> <gloss>rulers of essence</gloss>, that is, their own princes, whom they call **Fortune** or **Fate** <note>original: "εἱμαρμένη" (heimarmene)</note>. By these, all things are changed by the law of nature with the firmest stability, varied by eternal motion.

The air, however, is the instrument or the engine of all, through which all things are made. Its <term>ousiarches</term> <gloss>ruler of essence</gloss> is the **Second** <note>Likely referring to a secondary demiurgic power or the air itself as a mediating force.</note>. It provides mortal things to mortals and things similar to them.

Therefore, since these things are so, moving from the lowest to the highest, all things pertaining to themselves are so naturally connected to one another that mortal things are joined to mortals, and sensible things to sensibles. But the height of the government obeys that highest Lord, so that they are not many, but rather **one**. For all things hang from one, and rather flow down from Him. When they are seen at a distance, they are believed to be many and divided. But united, they are one, or rather two: that from which all things are made, and He by whom they are made. That is, from the matter out of which they are made, and from His will, by whose nod the others are brought to pass.

**ASCLEPIUS:** What is this reasoning again, O Trismegistus?

**TRISMEGISTUS:** It is such as this, O Asclepius. God, who is indeed either the Father or the Lord...

<summary>Trismegistus explains the hierarchy of divine rulers, from Jupiter in the heavens to the 'Omniform' ruler of the fixed stars and the planets of Fate, concluding that all things flow from a single divine source and its will.</summary>
<keywords>Jupiter, Ousiarches, Essence, Light, Sun, Horoscopes, Pantomorphos, Fate, Seven Spheres, Unity of God, Matter</keywords>

Indeed, arsenic can certainly by no means be fixed <note>made stable and non-volatile under heat</note> unless the practicing artist has an equal knowledge of its staining spirit <note>the volatile essence that imparts color or quality</note>, a point on which all the philosophers have slumbered, laboring in vain to produce anything from it. Therefore, whoever remains ignorant of this spirit should have no hope of fixing the substance itself, nor of attributing to it the power by which the perfection of transmutation is acquired. For this reason, I make it known to all that the whitening of which mention was made is drawn from a false foundation; by it, copper is falsely whitened but not truly changed. The Sophists have mixed <term>Venus</term> <gloss>copper</gloss> masked and painted in this manner with double its weight of <term>Luna</term> <gloss>silver</gloss>, and sold it to goldsmiths and coin-makers. Ultimately, however, they transformed themselves into counterfeiters—not only those who sold it, but also those who bought it. Some of the Sophists took red arsenic in place of the white, and this likewise vanished into a false art. For in whatever way it is prepared, it shows nothing but a white color. Others have proceeded further to common sulfur, which they cooked until yellow with vinegar, lye, or very sharp urine, day and night, until a white color emerged. Afterward, they raised it up from common salt and quicklime made from eggshells <note>original: "calce ouorum"</note> through sublimation; they cooked and sublimated it many times. Nevertheless, it always remained combustible, although white. With this, however, to fix crude mercury <unclear>20 lines of hieroglyphic text, not transcribed</unclear>

<summary>Paracelsus denounces the use of arsenic and sulfur in "sophistic" whitening processes that merely mask copper to look like silver. He warns that these methods lead to counterfeiting rather than true transmutation because the internal spirit of the mineral is not understood.</summary>
<keywords>arsenic, fixation, copper, silver, counterfeiting, sulfur, sublimation, quicklime, mercury, alchemy</keywords>

Our matter, however, is bought from no shop, yet it is found in such shops daily, and merchants cast it out into the streets. It is enough, therefore, that it may be found for free. But the matter of our <term>stone</term> <gloss>lapis</gloss> is compared to all those things with which the craftsmen work. For our stone is <term>our salt</term>, <term>our Mercury</term>, <term>verdigris</term> <gloss>rust of copper</gloss>, <term>halonitrum</term> <gloss>saltpeter</gloss>, <term>sal ammoniac</term>, <term>Mars</term> <gloss>iron</gloss>, <term>sulfur</term>, and infinite others of that kind. Yet it is not dug out from wild and rural mountains with hammers and other instruments. Our stone is drawn only from our own mountains and springs. In our <term>Salt-spring</term> <gloss>Salis-fonte</gloss> our <term>Salt</term> is found; from our earth our metal, <term>Mercury</term>, and <term>sulfur</term> are poured, and not from wild, foreign, and rural mountains. The craftsmen do not understand all these things, nor can they believe or comprehend them. For the Lord has darkened and stopped up their senses, for which reason they used these things otherwise than ought to be done, and did not aim at the mark at all. Nevertheless, they persisted in that contrary sense and followed their own stubborn heads. For instance, while they ought to <term>distill</term> gently, there they <term>sublimated</term> <gloss>vaporized to solid</gloss> with a strong fire, scorched <term>aqua fortis</term> <gloss>strong nitric acid</gloss>, and immediately burned the operation of nature and its substances, reducing them to nothing. Also, when they ought to <term>dissolve</term> <gloss>solvere</gloss>, there they <term>coagulated</term>; and again, as men unskilled in things, they handled the matter unskillfully. They fell into doubt and repeatedly claimed with lying words that the art was not true, but false, in which, however, they themselves deservedly lie. For their own ignorance shamefully deceived them, which is to be imputed to their own obscure and misty cunning, while, according to their own dark understanding, they interpreted the words differently than they sounded. For example, when the Philosophers spoke of <term>calcining</term> (which they call grinding), then those unskilled <term>pseudo-philosophers</term> <gloss>Philosophastri</gloss> understood it as burning, and reduced the things entirely to ashes, so that nothing could be made from them. Likewise, when the Philosophers <term>dissolve</term> or transmute into water, then those <term>know-it-alls</term> <gloss>nasutuli; literally 'big-noses'</gloss> burned nature with <term>strong water</term> <gloss>aqua forti</gloss>, and with that same water, which has no...

<summary>The author distinguishes between common chemical substances and the secret Hermetic matter, which is found everywhere but unrecognized by the ignorant. He criticizes unskilled practitioners for misinterpreting philosophical terms and using excessive heat which destroys the work.</summary>

requires temperance of the fire, and a succession of gradual increases with caution, until it is fixed in its lime <note>the oxide or powdered state</note>, lest it easily return into a body <note>revert to metallic form</note>, so that a greater fire may be administered to it for the perfection of its lime. Similarly, let him not happen to err in the case of <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>Tin</gloss>, because of the difficulty of its reduction; for if he should ever place its lime into reduction, it might happen that it does not reduce, but he finds it in its prior disposition or reduced into glass, and he might judge its reduction to be impossible. For we say that if one does not apply a great fire in the reduction of <term>Jupiter</term>, it will not reduce. If however a great fire is used, it does not necessarily happen that it reduces, but it is possible to reduce it into vitrification <note>turning into glass</note>. And this is because <term>Jupiter</term> <margin>am ta</margin> <margin>cc</margin> has a fugitive substance of <term>argentum vivum</term> <gloss>quicksilver or mercury</gloss> enclosed in the depth of its nature. If this remains for a long time in the fire, it will flee, and leave the body deprived of humidity, so that it is found to be converted more readily to vitrification than to the fusion of a metallic body. For everything deprived of its own humidity gives no fusion except a vitrifying one. Therefore, it necessarily remains that one must hasten to reduce it quickly with a most rapid impetus of fire. Otherwise it is not reduced. Let him therefore practice this, and he shall know. <margin>et</margin>

The <gloss>second</gloss> mode <margin>85, 6</margin> of calcination of these two bodies <gloss>Saturn and Jupiter</gloss>, which is perfected by the sharpness of salt, is that a quantity of salt be thrown upon their surface, quantity after quantity, very frequently during their fusion; and they should be mixed with much agitation by an iron rod over the fire, until through the mixing of the salt they are turned into ash. And afterwards, by the same method of perfection, their lime may be perfected according to its considerations. But in this there is also a difference in the calcination of these two bodies. Because <term>plumbum</term> <gloss>lead</gloss> is converted into powder from the first labors of calcination more easily than <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>tin</gloss>, yet its lime is not perfected more easily than that of <term>Jupiter</term>. The cause of this depends on the fact that <term>Saturn</term> <gloss>lead</gloss> has a more fixed humidity than <term>Jupiter</term>.

829. Since Religion resides in the highest parts of a man, and from the highest parts his lower parts live and shine, and because Mohammed <note>original: "Mahumedes"</note> is present in their minds along with their religion, a certain Mohammed is always placed in their sight. So that they may turn their faces toward the East, above which is the Lord, he is placed below the Christian center <note>original: "Meditullium"</note>. This is not the actual Mohammed who wrote the Quran <note>original: "Alcoranum"</note>, but another who performs his office; nor is it always the same person, for he is changed. Once it was a man from Saxony who, after being captured by Algerians, became a Mohammedan. Because he had also been a Christian, he was sometimes moved to speak with them about the Lord, saying that He was not the son of Joseph, but the Son of God Himself. Other Mohammeds succeeded this one later. In the place where this representative Mohammed has his seat, a fire appears like torches so that he may be identified; but that fire is not visible to any but the Mohammedans.

830. The actual Mohammed who wrote the Quran is not seen today. I was told that in early times he presided over them, but because he wished to rule over all things of their religion like a God, he was ejected from his seat (which he held beneath the Papists) and sent down to the right side near the south. Once, when a certain society of Mohammedans was stirred up by malicious spirits to acknowledge Mohammed as God, in order to settle the sedition, Mohammed was raised up from the lower earth and shown to them; and I also saw him then. He appeared similar to corporeal spirits who have no interior perception, with his face verging toward black, and I heard him speaking these words: *I am your Mohammed*; and soon he seemed to sink back down.

831. The Mohammedans are hostile to Christians primarily because of the belief in three Divine Persons, and consequently the worship of three Gods, as many Creators; and additionally toward the Roman Catholics because of their kneeling before images. Because of this, they call the latter Idolaters and the former fanatics, saying that they make God three-headed, and that they say "one" but mutter "three," and thus they split apart Omnipotence, making three out of the one and the unique. They say Christians are like Fauns with three horns, one for each God, and yet three for one, and that they thus pray, thus sing, and thus sound from their pulpits.

832. Like all nations who acknowledge one God, love what is just, and do good from a religious motive, the Mohammedans have their own Heaven, but outside the Christian one. However, the Mohammedan Heaven is divided into two. In the lower one, they live honestly with several wives; but no others are raised from there into the higher Heaven than those who renounce concubines and acknowledge the Lord our Savior, and at the same time His dominion over Heaven and Hell. I heard that it is impossible for them to think of God the Father and our Lord as being one, but that it is possible for them to believe that He rules over the Heavens and Hells because He is the Son of God the Father. This is the faith among them through which the Lord grants them ascent into the higher Heaven.

833. The fact that the Mohammedan religion is accepted by more kingdoms than the Christian religion can be a scandal <note>a cause for stumbling or doubt</note> to those who think about Divine Providence and at the same time believe that no one can be saved except those born Christian. But the Mohammedan religion is not a scandal to those who believe that all things are of Divine Providence; these people search for the reason why it is so, and they find it. It is in this: that the Mohammedan religion acknowledges the Lord as the Greatest Prophet, the Wisest of all, and also as the Son of God. But because they have made the Quran the only book of their religion, and consequently Mohammed, who wrote it, is seated in their thoughts and they follow him with some worship, they think little about our Lord. So that it may be fully known that this religion was raised up by the Divine Providence of the Lord to destroy the idolatries of many nations, it will be described in some order; but first, concerning the origin of idolatries. Before that religion, there was idolatrous worship.

It explains that Muslims can enter a higher heaven if they acknowledge the Lord's divinity and suggests their religion was providentially established to counter idolatry.</summary>
<keywords>Mohammedans, Mohammed, Quran, Trinity, Divine Providence, Spiritual World, Idolatry, Heaven</keywords>

plainly, the greatest part of diseases coming from celestial influence and from the Astral Impression of the Firmament of the Greater World <note>the Macrocosm or universe</note> do not wish to be cured with indiscriminate remedies, such as through the <term>Arcana</term> <gloss>secret essences</gloss> of herbs, minerals, or metals; rather, the cure should be established through Astronomical Influence using only those things which have an analogy to the greater and lesser world <note>the Microcosm or man</note>. They also made an image of the Head and Tail of the dragon of the Moon <note>referring to the lunar nodes, the points where the Moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic</note>, specifically the likeness of a serpent between the aerial and fiery circle, with the head of a hawk surrounding them, in the likeness of the Greek letter <term>theta</term> <gloss>θ</gloss>. They affirm that this image contributes much to the success of petitions, and they intended to signify a good and happy <term>daemon</term> <gloss>spirit or guiding intelligence</gloss> through it. They wished to represent him by the image of a serpent, for the Egyptians and Phoenicians celebrate this as a divine animal above all others, and they honor its divine nature because there exists in it a sharper spirit and a more abundant fire than in other animals. This is shown by its swift movement without any feet, hands, or other instruments, and also because it repeatedly renews its age with discarded skins and becomes young again. But they made the image of the Tail <note>the South Node</note> in a similar way when the Moon was eclipsed in the Tail, or was poorly affected by Saturn or Mars. They made it to induce anxiety and infirmity, and they called it an evil <term>genius</term> <gloss>guiding spirit</gloss>. A certain Hebrew had enclosed such an image in a golden and doubled belt which Blanche, daughter of the Duke of Bourbon, gave as a gift to her husband Peter, the first of that name, King of the Spains (whether she was aware of it or ignorant). When he was girded with it, he seemed to himself to be encircled by a serpent. Having later discovered the magic power inserted into the belt, he repudiated his wife for that reason.

In the sixth, to place love between two people, they sealed in white wax two images embracing each other, and fumigated it with aloe wood and amber. He refers here to the <term>vacuum</term> <gloss>void or empty space</gloss>, suggesting that the world could have occupied a different position within that vacuum. From this, he concluded that the world was created by an act of **Will**. The premise stating that the Will is what specifies one of two identical options is correct. However, the premise stating that the world is in a surrounding vacuum is false, or at least not self-evident. Furthermore, his assumption of this vacuum leads to a conclusion they consider abominable, which is that the vacuum would be eternal; for if it were created in time, it would itself require a vacuum <note>this leads to an infinite regress of spaces needed for space to exist in</note>.

As for the premise stating that nothing but a time-bound object of will can result from the Will, this is not self-evident. This is because the **Will in act** <note>the actualized exercise of will</note> is simultaneous with the action upon the object of will itself. This is because the Will belongs to the category of **relational terms** <note>original: *al-muḍāf*</note>. It has been demonstrated that when one of two relational terms exists in act, the other must exist in act, such as father and son; and if one exists in potentiality, the other exists in potentiality. Therefore, if the Will in act is created in time, then the **object of will** <note>original: *al-murād*</note> must necessarily be created in time. But if the Will in act is eternal, then the object of will in act is eternal.

As for the Will that precedes the object of will, that is the **Will in potentiality** <note>original: *al-irāda bi-al-quwwa*</note>. This means the object of its will has not yet emerged into actuality because the action necessitated for the occurrence of the object was not yet joined to that Will. Therefore, it is clear that when its object of will does emerge, it exists in a state of being in which it did not exist before the object emerged into actuality, since the Will was the cause of the object’s occurrence through the mediation of the action. Thus, if the **Theologians** <note>original: *al-Mutakallimūn*, scholars of Kalam or speculative theology</note> were to posit that the Will is created in time, it would necessarily follow that the object of will is created in time.

The apparent meaning of the **Divine Law** <note>original: *al-Shar‘*, referring to the religious texts and revelation</note> is that it did not engage in this level of depth with the general public. For this reason, it did not explicitly state whether the Will is eternal or created in time. Rather, it stated what is most apparent: that the Will brings created beings into existence. This is found in the words of the Exalted: 

->Verily, Our word unto a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say unto it: **Be**, and it is.<- <note>Quran 16:40</note>

So it is handed down that if a living Duck is applied to the belly during colics, the disease passes into it, and the duck dies. Archytas <note>Archytas of Tarentum, a Greek philosopher and mathematician of the Pythagorean school</note> says something similar: if a heart recently extracted from an animal, still warm and beating, is hung over a patient with a quartan fever <note>a fever occurring at intervals of three days, historically associated with malaria</note>, it removes it. Likewise, if anyone swallows the heart of a Hoopoe, or a Swallow, or a Weasel, or a Mole while it is still alive and pulsating, it confers upon him memory, recollection, intellect, and divination. 

From this has arisen a general precept: namely, that whatever things are to be collected from animals—whether stones, members, or excrements such as hair, dung, or claws—these should be taken from those animals while they are still living, and even, if possible, while they remain alive afterward. For this reason they instruct that when you collect the tongue of a Frog, you should return the living frog to the water; if you collect a tooth or an eye of a Wolf, you should not kill the Wolf; and so on with similar things. 

Democritus <note>The ancient Greek philosopher, often cited in later magical texts for his supposed knowledge of the secrets of nature</note> relates that if anyone extracts the tongue of a living sea-frog <note>original: "Ranæ marinæ"; likely referring to a Lophius or anglerfish</note> with no other part of the body adhering to it, and after the frog is returned to the sea, places the tongue over the heart-palpitation of a sleeping woman, she will answer truthfully to whatever questions he asks. In a similar way, they promise that the eyes of frogs, tied to a sick person before sunrise such that the frogs are released blind into the water, drive away tertian fevers <note>fever that recurs every other day</note>. They also hand down that these same eyes, tied in a deer skin with the flesh of a Nightingale, grant wakefulness and drive away sleep. Similarly, the barb of a Stingray <note>original: "Pastinacæ radius"; the stinging spine of the common stingray</note> tied to the navel is said to make births easy.

What need is there to search for many things regarding this matter in his law and his prophets? Rather, there is no need to search; for they are not obscure or erased, but plain and frequent to collect and to place in this my disputation, by which it appears clearer than light: that he, the true and supreme God, willed that sacrifice be offered to none at all except to himself. Behold this one thing, briefly or rather grandly, threateningly, but truly said by that God whom their most learned men preach as so excellent: let it be heard, let it be feared, let it be fulfilled, lest the rooting out of the disobedient follow. He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, he says, save to the Lord only. Not because he has need of anything, but because it is profitable for us that we be his property. ### The Parable of the Wheat

A parable of a man who lived in the wilderness </note><note>original: *beini davrin*</note> and did not know the customs of the city. He sowed wheat and ate the wheat in its raw state. One day he entered the city, and they offered him a good bread. He said: "What is this for?" They said: "It is bread to eat." He ate it and found it very pleasant to his taste. **The Rabbi said**: "From what is this made?" They said: "From wheat." Later they brought him cakes kneaded in oil. He tasted them and said: "And what are these made of?" They said: "From wheat." Later they brought him royal pastries made with honey and oil. He said: "And what are these delicacies made of?" They said: "From wheat." He said: "Certainly I am the master of all these things, for I eat the essence of all these, which is wheat." And because of that...

# Chapter 2

## Tractate Bikkurim Chapter 2 Mishnah 1
->1<-
The heave offering <term>terumah</term> <note>the portion of the harvest given to the Priests</note> and the first fruits <term>bikkurim</term>
share several laws:
One is liable for the death penalty <note>at the hands of Heaven</note> and an additional fifth <note>if eaten accidentally by a non-priest, they must pay back the value plus twenty percent</note> for eating them;
they are forbidden to laypeople <term>zarim</term> <note>anyone who is not a Priest/Kohen</note>;
they are the property of the Priest;
they are neutralized <note>if accidentally mixed with common food</note> in a ratio of one to one hundred;
and they require the washing of hands and the setting of the sun <note>a Priest who was impure must immerse in a ritual bath and wait until sunset before he can eat them</note>.
These rules apply to <term>terumah</term> and <term>bikkurim</term>,
which is not the case for the tithe <term>ma'aser</term> <note>referring here specifically to the Second Tithe, which is eaten by the owner in Jerusalem</note>.

## Tractate Bikkurim Chapter 2 Mishnah 2
->2<-
There are rules applying to the tithe and the first fruits which do not apply to the heave offering:
For the tithe and the first fruits require being brought to a specific place <note>Jerusalem</note>;
they require a formal declaration <term>viddui</term> <note>the Tithe confession or the First Fruits declaration</note>;
and they are forbidden to an <term>onen</term> <note>a person in the first day of mourning for a close relative</note>;
Rabbi Shimon permits an <term>onen</term> to eat them.
They are subject to the law of removal <term>bi'ur</term> <note>the requirement to clear all tithes from the house in the third and sixth years of the sabbatical cycle</note>.
Rabbi Shimon exempts them.
And any amount of them <note>even a tiny mixture</note> is forbidden to be eaten outside of Jerusalem,
and their offshoots <note>crops grown from their seeds</note> are forbidden to be eaten in Jerusalem,
even for laypeople and for livestock.
Rabbi Shimon permits these.
These rules apply to the tithe and the first fruits,
which is not the case for the heave offering.

### **Torah** is Light
These commandments mentioned in this Torah portion are divided into three parts, which are the three pillars upon which the world stands: Torah, Service <note>worship/sacrifices</note>, and Acts of Loving-kindness.

**Torah** consists of the prohibitions: "You shall not add" and "You shall not subtract" <note>Deuteronomy 13:1</note>, which indicate the perfection of the Torah. This is as the philosophers say: a thing that is absolutely perfect cannot be said to be lacking or excessive. For if it were lacking, it would not be perfect; and if it could accept an addition, it would mean it was not previously complete. Therefore, the definition of the "Perfect" is that which has neither deficiency nor excess. It is known that the Torah is suspended upon His Great Name, which is <term>Y-H-V-H</term> <gloss>the Tetragrammaton</gloss>, for "The Torah of the Lord <note>Y-H-V-H</note> is perfect," as I have elaborated in my work on Tractate Shavuot in the chapter "Torah Ohr." 

As it is written in the Zohar on the verse "This is My Name and this is My Memorial" <note>Exodus 3:15</note>: The letters <term>Yod-He</term> with "My Name" <note>Hebrew: Shemi</note> equals 365 <note>the number of negative commandments</note>. The letters <term>Vav-He</term> with "My Memorial" <note>Hebrew: Zichri</note> equals 248 <note>the number of positive commandments</note>. It is also written: "I am the first and I am the last" <note>Isaiah 44:6</note>. He is the Absolute Perfection, containing no subtraction or addition. Regarding this comes the warning: "You shall not do so unto the Lord your God" <note>Deuteronomy 12:4</note>, which is a warning against erasing the Name or shattering a stone from the Holy Temple. Behold, the letters of the Name are like the house in which He, may He be blessed, dwells; and so too is the Sanctuary. It is written: "I am the Lord, that is My Name" <note>Isaiah 42:8</note>; the letters are like a frame for the house, and His Name, may He be blessed, is the soul within them. One who destroys His "house," as it were, destroys Him. This is the secret of "You shall not do so unto the Lord your God."

**Service** <note>original: "avodah"</note> comprises the majority of the commandments mentioned in this portion. The command came to have a fixed place in the Chosen House, and the text gives the reason: "To His habitation shall you seek, and there shall you come" <note>Deuteronomy 12:5</note>. "To His habitation" <note>original: "leshichno"</note> hints at the <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss>, which is the palace of the Name <term>Yod-He-Vav-He</term>. Do not fear that She dwells there, for in the Sanctuary, the Glory <note>original: "Kavod"</note> is unified with Beauty <note>original: "Tiferet"</note> among His people. This is the meaning of "to place His Name there," which the Targum renders as "to cause His Presence to dwell." Around the place of holiness, "the wicked walk on every side" <note>Psalm 12:9</note>, referring to the <term>Kelipot</term> <gloss>husks/forces of impurity</gloss>. Therefore: "Take heed to yourself lest you offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see" <note>Deuteronomy 12:13</note>.

### **Sometimes**
Spark of holiness spread outward, and it is a commandment to return them and bring them within. This is the secret of the commandment to bring the firstborn and the sacrifices from outside the city to the Chosen House. Then the branch returns to its root. It is written regarding them: "There you shall ascend," meaning there they shall have an elevation <note>original: "aliyah"</note> and not outside. 

Since holiness resides in the Chosen House, which is in the Holy Land, we are commanded to "turn away from evil" by destroying all the places where the nations worshipped. One must uproot and eradicate them. This was commanded specifically in the Holy Land. The secret of this hints that the [other] nations are not [merely] idolaters; rather, the nations in the Land of Israel, being under the direct rule of the Glorious Name, serve God by "cutting the plantings" <note>a metaphor for heresy</note>, which is true idolatry. However, outside the Land, they are under the rule of external forces. Just as there is a great prohibition against shattering a single stone of holiness, so conversely, it is a great commandment to destroy and eliminate a "Subverted City" <note>original: "ir hanidachat"</note> and never to rebuild it, for its place is impure. 

Similarly, with the one who entices <note>original: "mesit"</note> or misleads others [to idolatry], one must uproot and eradicate him, for he stems from the impurity of the Primordial Serpent who was the first enticer. The Holy One, blessed be He, immediately said: "Cursed is the serpent." Therefore, the powers of <term>Sammael</term> <gloss>the angel of evil</gloss> are never healed. The command came not to love him and not to listen to him, similar to what was said of the serpent: "And I will put enmity between you and the woman" <note>Genesis 3:15</note>. A false prophet is also like an enticer. 

Let us return to the matter: the root of holiness is the Chosen House and Jerusalem. This is the reason for the first fruits <note>original: "bikkurim"</note>, which the priests have no permission to eat until they are placed in the Chosen House. For the first fruits, being the "beginning," indicate a great holiness. Therefore, they must go to the holy place, and from there they take their wisdom, for they are "holy unto God," and they shall eat in Jerusalem. 

This is the secret of the "Lesser Sanctuaries" and the "Second Tithe" <note>original: "ma'aser sheni"</note>, whose consumption is in Jerusalem. This is the "blessing of grain, wine, and oil," which are the primary ancestors of all sustenance. It is forbidden to eat the lesser sacrifices until after the sprinkling of their blood, for the blood is the soul <note>original: "nefesh"</note>. Afterward, there is permission to enjoy them. Know that just as the Service—which is the sacrifice—is an offering to God, so too is the worshiper. For the essence of the Service is that a person sacrifices himself, according to the secret of: "When a man <note>original: "Adam"</note> offers of himself" <note>Leviticus 1:2</note>. The burnt offering <note>original: "olah"</note> is entirely consumed, for it comes to atone for the thoughts of the mind, which is spiritual. It is offered all night so the serpent cannot hinder it. The lesser sacrifices are for the peace of the soul and the body.

### **The Secret of the Firstborn**
This is the secret of the "Holy Israel," who are called "the firstborn of Israel." God has pity on them and guards them, and they are called "the sheep of My pasture." Therefore, [the firstborn animal] is eaten only by the priests. The secret of eating sacrifices corresponds to their blemishes and foundations. For Israel is holy and Israel is called "Man" <note>original: "Adam"</note>. He was holy, but later a blemish fell upon him after he sinned, and he was clothed in "garments of skin." But he has a redemption, through the secret of "I will give a man in your stead." This was the secret of the <term>Azazel</term> <gloss>scapegoat</gloss>, which "bore their iniquities." Their iniquities rest upon its head and upon its people. But we are commanded not to cause a blemish in a sanctified animal in order to eat it. For if one intentionally blemishes the sanctified, he also violates the prohibition of labor and shearing with consecrated animals, for even the "broken tablets" <note>of the Ten Commandments</note> remain holy.

### **The General Principle**
The Service is the sacrifice, but the internal sacrifice is the Man himself. Likewise, his soul is called to the "Altar on High" after his death, and Michael is the High Priest. This is the secret, for "in the image of God was Man made." Therefore, the warning was given to be careful during his life regarding damages to the soul, not to kill a person except after thorough searching and investigation. Then, his death is "at the hands of Heaven," following the secret that "He is the witness and He is the judge." For the Lord, may He be blessed, is a True Witness and a True Judge. So too must the Sanhedrin be: just as they are true judges, they must have true witnesses. I mean that they must clarify the truth of the testimony with complete clarity—namely, searching and investigation—and then their judgment is like the judgment of Heaven. "Precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death [of His pious ones]" <note>Psalm 116:15</note>.

### **Since the Death**
Of the pious is precious in the eyes of God—for Israel is holy from the side of their souls, and after death their souls cleave above—therefore the command came: "You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness [for the dead]" <note>Deuteronomy 14:1</note>, because "you are children to the Lord your God." This is not the case for the [idolatrous] nations. Laceration and baldness are their customs, and rightly so, since at their death they go to destruction and have no portion in this world or the World to Come. We, however, are children of God. When we depart from this world—which is a temporary dwelling—on the contrary, we have a permanent residence above with our Father in Heaven. Therefore, it is forbidden to mourn excessively or perform these actions.

### **Let us return to the matter**
The person who worships is himself the sacrifice, as it says: "When a man offers of himself." There is another secret here: even when a man descends below, specifically through the secret of <term>Gilgul</term> <gloss>reincarnation/transmigration of souls</gloss>—"Man and beast You save, O Lord" <note>Psalm 36:7</note>. Therefore, even regarding the eating of non-consecrated meat <note>original: "basar ta'avah"</note>, we were commanded regarding ritual slaughter <note>original: "shechitah"</note> with great caution, ensuring no nick [in the blade]. If there is a nick, the animal becomes "carrion" <note>original: "nevelah"</note>, and then a "vile thing" <note>nevalah</note> is done in Israel. For who knows what soul is transmigrated within it? "Love your fellow as yourself" <note>Leviticus 19:18</note>—select for him a "beautiful death," namely, slaughter without a nick. If the animal dies on its own, the power of impurity takes hold of it. But when one slaughters it properly, and the animal or pure bird contains a spark of holiness, its soul departs in purity.

### **One who eats a limb from a living animal**
Is like one who eats the flesh of the soul when a transmigrated soul is present. This is the secret of "You shall not eat the soul with the flesh." Likewise, the prohibition of forbidden foods and the signs of pure animals, beasts, and birds all indicate the spark spread within them—whether it is from the "Side of Impurity" <note>original: "Sitra Achra"</note> or the "Side of Holiness." I elaborated on this in Parashat Shemini. When Israel conducts themselves with holiness, it is written of them: "And they shall make for Me a sanctuary, and I will dwell within them" <note>Exodus 25:8</note>. They themselves are the Tabernacle. For Man is divided into three parts: the head corresponds to the Holy of Holies; the heart corresponds to the Holy Place; and from the belly downward corresponds to the Courtyard. I elaborated on this in Parashat Terumah. When one eats foods that are from the side of holiness, they are like sacrifices offered upon the Altar. Regarding this, our Sages said: "Now, a person's table atones for him," as I elaborated in its place.

### **Regarding the Festivals**
And their sacrifices, I have written about each in its specific place. The command came to rejoice on the festivals and to ascend for the pilgrimage: "Three times a year all your males shall appear." Do not read it only as "appearing" [to God], but also as "being seen" [by God]. Therefore, if one wishes to be seen in the Holy Temple where the Glory dwells, he must "turn from evil and do good" and be a faithful servant to his Creator. Otherwise, it is forbidden to "tread in My courts, O wicked one." How can he wish to be seen before God while bringing a burnt offering of appearance? He himself becomes a sacrifice through the sacrifice he offers. It says: "Three times a year he shall appear"—like Isaac, who was a "perfect burnt offering."

### On the shame sought from unworthy praises.
## DIALOGUE XXVI.

> Praise sparingly, for when you praise unjustly,

Hence they are even more prone than is right toward praising; and although I admit it is bad to praise the unworthy, yet to criticize the undeserving is much worse.

*Sorrow.* I praised an unworthy man.

*Reason.* If you did so knowingly, you are blameworthy; but if unknowingly, you are excusable. It is a lesser evil to be deceived than to deceive. For to be deceived is the fault of another; but to deceive is the specific crime of the deceiver.

## On the Motion of the Heart, etc.

Since these things are so, it is established that another point I previously stated will also be confirmed: namely, that the blood passes continually through the heart. For we see in the external appearance of the body that the blood flows from the arteries into the veins, not from the veins into the arteries. We see, moreover, that almost the entire mass of the blood can be drained from the arm itself (and this by a single skin-vein opened with a scalpel, if a proper ligature is applied). We see, furthermore, that it is poured out so impetuously and abundantly that it is clear that not only is the blood which was contained in the arm below the ligature before the incision quickly and rapidly evacuated, but also the blood from the whole arm and the whole body, from both the arteries and the veins.

Therefore, it must first be acknowledged that the blood is supplied by force and impulse, and is driven by force <note>The Latin "impingi" suggests a forceful striking or driving forward of the fluid.</note>

**The one in which.** "The black." He mentioned the black because the time of the kingdom of Babylon had already passed. And the kingdom of Media and Persia went out first toward the north country because they were in everything to destroy it, and afterward they ruled over all the kingdoms of the earth.

"And the white," which is the kingdom of Greece, "went out after them" because the kingdom was divided. For Alexander of Macedon <note>Alexander the Great</note>, the first king of Greece, killed Darius in Babylon and took the kingdom from him and reigned; and afterward his successors ruled throughout the whole world.

**And the dappled went out toward the south country.** These were the Roman portion, because Rome is <unclear>shnunith</unclear>, and Augustus Caesar, who ruled over Rome, began to fight against the kingdom of Greece. At the start of his wars, he went out to the land of Egypt, which is in the south, and in all those lands the Greeks were ruling then. **And the strong.** These are a hint to the kingdom of Ishmael <note>the Arab/Islamic conquests</note>, who strengthened themselves of their own accord to seek a kingdom, to have a place that would be settled for them. **And he said.** That is to say, he gave them permission to walk and to conquer lands.

**And he cried out.** That is to say, he called to me with a great voice and said to me, **"See, those that go toward the north country have quieted my spirit in the north country."** This refers to the portion of the black horses who went out to Babylon to destroy it.

The person undergoing evacuation must not rush into eating large amounts of harmful foods, lest nature attract them before they are digested. If any of that is necessary, it must be taken little by little, spaced out so it occurs gradually, ensuring that what enters the body is well-digested. Bloodletting <term>al-fasd</term> is the evacuation specific to equalizing the balance <note>of the blood</note>. As for the evacuation specific to a humor that is excessive in quantity or corrupt in quality, it is something other than bloodletting. Every excessive evacuation usually causes vomiting. 

If someone suffers from the cessation of a habitual diarrhea, this becomes a cause for the recurrence of that evacuation, which usually builds up. For instance, if the cessation causes a blockage or a nasal congestion, the return of the evacuation causes it to disappear. Know that the remainder of the matter which requires evacuation is less receptive to total extraction; pushing to reach total exhaustion may cause the patient’s strength to fail. Nature often dissolves that remainder on its own. As long as the humor is of the type intended and the patient can bear it, do not fear the excess; you may even need to evacuate until the patient faints <note>original: "al-ghashi"</note>. 

If a person has strong physical power but a large amount of bad humors, evacuate them little by little. Likewise, if the matter is highly mature <note>concocted</note> or heavily mixed with the blood, it cannot be evacuated all at once. This occurs in cases of sciatica, chronic joint pain, cancer, chronic scabies, and chronic boils. Know that purging <term>al-ishal</term> draws from above and uproots from below, so it aligns with the customary attraction <note>of waste</note> and is also suitable after the materials have settled. If the materials are below, it draws them to itself by opposition and uproots them from where they are. 

Bloodletting varies in its state according to the locations from which the blood is taken, as you have learned. The people who least need evacuation are those with good digestion; residents of hot countries also have little need for evacuation. 

We say: it is recommended for whoever wishes to take a purgative to restrict or divide their food steadily. First, determine the amount to be tested in a day across several doses, making them of different foods and different drinks. This state causes the stomach to desire to push what is in it either upward or downward. As for uniform food <note>without variety</note>, the stomach becomes saturated by it, digests it slowly, and grips it tightly, especially if the quantity is small. For those with a naturally loose bowel, none of this is necessary. 

Know that the need for vomiting, purging, and the like does not occur for one who follows a good regimen <term>husn al-tadbir</term>; such a person needs only what is lighter than that. Perhaps exercise, massage, and cupping will suffice for them. If the body becomes overfilled with the best of humors—meaning blood—then bloodletting is what is needed for its purification, rather than purging. If necessity dictates bloodletting or evacuation, such as in the autumn, begin with bloodletting then follow with vomiting; this is among the counsels of Hippocrates <note>original: "Abiqrat"</note> and the writings of Apollo, and it is the truth. 

Likewise, if phlegmatic humors are mixed with the blood, bloodletting may increase their thickness and viscosity if the humors are equal, viscous, and cold. In such a case, one must begin with purging. In general, if the humors are equal, prioritize bloodletting; if an excess remains after that, then evacuate. If they are unequal, evacuate the excess first until they are equal, then perform bloodletting. Whoever puts medicine before bloodletting should perform the bloodletting a few days prior. If someone has recently undergone bloodletting and needs evacuation, drinking medicine will be more effective for them. Often, drinking medicine when bloodletting was what was required results in vomiting and distress; if it does not settle with sedatives, it is because bloodletting should have preceded it. 

There is no evacuation required for excessive fullness that is more urgent than what is called for by the severity of the illness and the fullness in terms of quality and quantity. Often, good regimen takes the place of a bloodletting that was necessary at the time. Often, a call for evacuation arises but is countered by an obstacle, in which case the only trick is fasting, sleep, and correcting the imbalance caused by the fullness. 

Some evacuation is done by way of precaution <term>al-istizhar</term>, such as what is needed by those prone to gout, epilepsy, or other conditions at a known time, especially in the spring. One needs to take precautions before the time and perform the specific evacuation, whether it be bloodletting or purging. Sometimes the use of external drying agents and desiccating medicines acts as an evacuation, such as what is done for those with dropsy. 

You may need to use a medicine that matches the humor being evacuated in quality, such as scammony <term>saqmunia</term> when you need to evacuate yellow bile. In that case, you must mix it with what opposes it in quality but agrees with it in purging, such as myrobalan <term>halilaj</term>. If a bad temperament occurs afterward in those with abdominal tumors, their purging becomes weak. If you are forced to treat them, use things like bindweed <term>lablab</term> and safflower <term>qartham</term>. As for the purgative and purging cassia <term>khiyar shanbar</term>, Hippocrates said: whoever is naturally inclined to vomit, the primary way to purify them is to use emetics in the summer or spring, for that protects the body from fatigue. 

Know that for one who has a naturally loose bowel or is not accustomed to vomiting, they should avoid it unless necessary. One must thicken <note>the humor</note> before purging and vomiting by thinning the humor intended for evacuation and widening the passages. Know that for one with thin or weak abdominal walls <term>hazaal al-maraaq</term>, vomiting and purging are difficult and exhausting. An emetic medicine may turn into a purgative if the stomach is strong, or if it is drunk during intense hunger, or if the drinker has a naturally loose bowel, or because the medicine is of a heavy substance that descends quickly. Conversely, a purgative becomes an emetic due to the weakness of the stomach, or extreme heaviness, or because the medicine is repulsive to the patient, or if the patient has indigestion. 

Every purgative medicine, if it does not purge due to lack of maturation <note>of the humors</note>, will instead stir up the humor it was meant to purge and spread it through the body, overcoming the system and drawing other humors toward it, thus increasing that humor in the body. Some humors respond more quickly to vomiting, such as yellow bile; others are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile. Some require specific conditions, like phlegm, where purging is inherently more correct. 

For those whose humor is descending, such as those with "slippery intestines" <term>zalaq al-am'a</term>, the intestines grip, making purgative medicines difficult. This is often due to a medicine composed of widely varying ingredients in terms of purging time, causing the purging to be disturbed; the first ingredient might purge the second before the second can act. If someone undergoes purging and their body is clean, they will inevitably suffer from medicine-induced colic and distress, and the evacuation will be very difficult. In general, when medicine evacuates waste, there is no distress; if it is taken with distress, it is either evacuating something other than waste, or the humor being evacuated has changed, indicating the body is purified of the intended humor.

They descend into ritual impurity through thought, but they do not ascend <note>become pure again</note> except through a physical action. For an action can cancel out both a previous action and a previous thought, but a thought cannot cancel out either a previous action or a previous thought. And if we say that these items are for the purpose of eating, then through thought they should become ready <note>susceptible to impurity</note> and through thought they should be removed? But did we not learn in a Mishnah: * All handles of food items that are in a stack <note>Hebrew: <term>siman</term></note> on the threshing floor are pure <note>not susceptible to impurity as they are not considered handles yet</note>, but Rabbi Jose deems them impure. Here too, it refers to the literal herb. If so, what is the reason of the Rabbis? For they say like Rabbi Jose, as we learned: * Rabbi Jose deems them impure. Now, this is understandable there, for the reason of Rabbi Jose is according to Rabbi Simeon ben Lakish; for Rabbi Simeon ben Lakish said: Since they are fit to be turned over with a pitchfork <note>Hebrew: <term>atar</term></note>. But here <note>regarding Sukkah boards</note>, what are they fit for? It can be said they are for catching the fallen grain. As to the matter itself: All handles of food items that are in a stack on the threshing floor are pure, and Rabbi Jose deems them impure. Simeon ben Lakish asked: What is the meaning of <term>siman</term>? Rabbi Johanan said it means the literal plant. Rabbi Eleazar said: It refers to a pitchfork. Rabbi Eleazar said: Why is the prayer of the righteous compared to a pitchfork <note>Hebrew: <term>atar</term>, a wordplay on "to entreat"</note>? To tell you: just as this pitchfork turns the grain on the threshing floor from place to place, so too the prayer of the righteous turns the mind of the Holy One, Blessed be He, from the attribute of cruelty to the attribute of mercy.

Gemara: Rav said: The Mishnah's dispute <note>between Rabbi Judah and Rabbi Meir</note> is regarding roofing with boards. Rabbi Meir holds that if a board is four handbreadths wide, all agree it is invalid; but if it is less than four, there is a dispute. Rabbi Judah holds that even if it is four handbreadths wide, it is valid provided one does not sleep under it. Gemara: Rav said: The dispute is regarding boards that have a width of four; all agree that if it is four wide, it is invalid? Even less than that, they are just ordinary reeds! Rav Papa said: This is what he meant: If they are four handbreadths wide, all agree it is invalid. If they are less than three, all agree it is valid, as they are just like reeds. Where they disagree is from three to four handbreadths. One Master <note>Rabbi Meir</note> holds that since they do not have the minimum legal size for a "place," we do not decree against them. And the other Master <note>Rabbi Judah</note> holds that since they look like a permanent ceiling, we do decree against them. Do you think this represents everyone's view? No, the latter part of the ruling follows Rabbi Meir. Come and hear: * Two sheets join together...

For if he judges that those things which are avoidable will occur, then it is impossible for them to happen as he foresees; and if he is mistaken, which is not only wicked to believe but even to speak of. But if he discerns that they will happen just as they are, so that he knows they are able either to happen or not to happen, what kind of foreknowledge is this, which grasps nothing certain and nothing stable? # Question 85

### Article 3: Whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual knowledge.

Regarding the third point, the procedure is as follows. It seems that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual knowledge. For those things which are prior and better known according to nature are posterior and less known according to us; but universals are prior according to the nature of our intellect. Furthermore, composite things are prior as far as we are concerned, rather than simple things; but universals are simpler, therefore they are known later by us. Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the Physics that the defined thing comes first in our knowledge, and the parts of the definition are less universal: just as "animal" is part of the definition of "man," and so universals are known later by us. Furthermore, we arrive at effects by chance and principles; but universals are known later by us.

On the contrary is what is said in the first book of the Physics, that we must proceed from universals to singulars.

I respond that it must be said that in the knowledge of our intellect two things must be considered. First, indeed, that intellectual knowledge in some way takes its beginning from sensitive knowledge; and because the sense is of singulars and the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the knowledge of singulars as far as we are concerned be prior to the knowledge of universals. Second, we must consider that our intellect proceeds from <term>potentia</term> <gloss>potentiality</gloss> to <term>actus</term> <gloss>actuality</gloss>. And that which proceeds from potentiality to actuality first reaches an incomplete act, which is halfway between potentiality and act, and then a perfect act. The perfect act to which the intellect arrives is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; the incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is known in this way is known both in act and in a way in potentiality. As stated in the first book of the Physics: things which are more confused are first manifest and certain to us; later, however, we know by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly. It is manifest, moreover, that to know something in which many things are contained without having proper knowledge of each of those contained within it is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, both the whole in which parts are contained in potentiality and the integral whole can be known; for either whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being distinctly known. To know distinctly that which is contained in the whole is to have knowledge of a less common thing: just as to know "animal" indistinctly is to know "animal" in which is contained both rational and irrational, which is to know "man" or "lion." Therefore, it occurs first to our intellect to know "animal" before knowing "man." And this reasoning holds if we compare whatever is more [universal] to the less [universal]. As the sense goes from potentiality to act, so does the intellect.

<column-break/>

This order of knowledge appears in the sense. For we judge more by sense <unclear>...</unclear> and when the less is known in more remote things <note>referring to distance of perception</note> it is perceived to be a body; then it is perceived to be an animal; and further it is perceived to be a animal, and then a man, and finally Socrates. Or it is clear that children from the beginning first distinguish a man from a non-man; and in the beginning children call all men "fathers." Later, however, they distinguish each one individually, as is said in the first book of the Physics. Those things are manifest which one knows indistinctly and yet in potentiality, whether one knows the principle, so one knows the genus and is able to know the differences. And thus, in itself, indistinct knowledge is the middle between potentiality and act. And thus the knowledge of singulars is prior as far as we are concerned in sensitive knowledge, but the knowledge of the more universal is prior in intellectual knowledge.

To the first, it must be said that this can be considered in two ways. In one way, regarding the intention of truth. Since the intention of truth and the true is the same, it has a relation to many. This occurs by the abstraction of the intellect <unclear>...</unclear> so that it is truly posterior. In the first book On the Soul <note>Aristotle, De Anima</note>, it is said that the universal is either nothing or it is posterior; but <unclear>...</unclear> he placed universals as substances; and in this consideration it is true, because particulars are not except by participation in the more universal subsisting things which are called Ideas. In another way, it can be considered regarding the nature itself of "animality" or "humanity" as it is found in particulars. And thus there is a twofold order of nature. One according to the way of generation and time, since in that way things which are imperfect and in potentiality are prior; and in this way the more [universal] is prior in nature, which appears manifestly in the generation of man and animal. For first the animal is generated, then the man, as is said in the book On the Generation of Animals. The other is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as act is simply prior in nature, because through the perfect the imperfect is made; and in this way the less [universal] is prior in nature, as man is prior to animal. The intention of nature does not stop at the generation of the animal, but intends to generate the man.

To the second, the more universal is compared to the less universal as a whole, because the more universal contains in potentiality not only the man but also the horse. <note>The genus "animal" contains the species "man" and "horse".</note> Thus "animal" considered in itself is prior in our knowledge to "man."

To the third, it must be said that something can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely as it is in itself. In another way, as parts of this whole; as with stones, it is necessary that we first know the whole [house] before the parts. For we first know the house in a certain confused way. Thus it should be said that the defining parts, considered absolutely, are prior to the thing defined. Otherwise the defined thing would not be made known through them. But more [universals] are like parts.

<summary>Thomas Aquinas discusses the order of human cognition, arguing that the intellect proceeds from confused, universal concepts to distinct, specific knowledge. He differentiates between the order of nature (where the perfect is prior) and the order of human learning (where the general precedes the particular).</summary>

The Lion said: "I shall not be angry, so say what you wish."

She said: "I see that you do not recognize what harms you from what benefits you. I believe that by prolonging your consideration of Dimna's case, he will stir up against you a trouble that you will be unable to withstand or overcome."

Then she stood and left in anger. On the following day, the Judge sent for Dimna and brought him out. He consulted the scholars regarding him, but they said nothing.

The Judge said to him: "Even if everyone present remains silent and says nothing, their suspicions have united in the belief that you are a criminal. There is no good for you in life after this accusation has settled in their hearts. I see nothing better for you than to confess your sin; thus, you may free your neck from the consequences of the Hereafter, and a good reputation regarding your case may return to you for two reasons. The first is your ability to find exits and fabricate excuses <note>original: "al-ma'adhir"</note> to defend yourself. The second is your confession of your sin, choosing safety in the Hereafter over safety in this world. For scholars have said: Death in what is honorable is better than life in what is ugly."

Dimna answered him, saying: "Judges do not rule based on their own suspicions, nor on the suspicions of the common people or the elite. I have learned that suspicion is of no avail against the truth. Even if you all suspect that I am the author of this crime, I know myself, and my knowledge of myself is a certainty in which there is no doubt. My case has only become ugly in your souls because you suspected that I acted with malice."

Anxiety fell upon the entire court of <term>Tirmidh</term> <gloss>a city in Central Asia</gloss>; suspicion stirred within that Sultan as well.

If a woman leaves two sisters and a husband <note>The text specifies a husband but the context of "two sisters and a woman" suggests a female deceased</note> and bequeaths to a man the equivalent of a sister's portion minus one-eighth of what remains of the estate after the legacy. The calculation for this is that you establish the <term>fara'id</term> <gloss>legal inheritance shares</gloss> from twelve shares, where each sister receives one-third of what remains of the estate after the legacy. This is the estate minus the legacy. You know that one-eighth of what remains plus the legacy equals a sister's portion. One-eighth of what remains is one-eighth of the estate minus one-eighth of the legacy. So, one-eighth of the estate minus one-eighth of the legacy, plus the legacy, equals a sister's portion. That is one-eighth of the estate and seven-eighths of the legacy. The entire estate then equals three-eighths of the estate plus three legacies and five-eighths of a legacy. Subtract three-eighths of the estate from the total estate, and there remains five-eighths of the estate equaling three legacies and five-eighths of a legacy. The entire estate then equals five legacies and four-fifths of a legacy. Thus, the estate is twenty-nine, the legacy is five, and the portion is eight.

In another type of legacy: a man dies and leaves four sons and bequeaths to a man the equivalent of one of his sons' portions, and to another man one-quarter of what remains of the third. Know that the legacy is taken only from the third.

Just as a judge who is ignorant of the <term>Sunnah</term> <gloss>the body of social and legal custom and practice of the Islamic community</gloss> is not excused if he errs in a ruling, so too the one who passes judgment on existing things without meeting the conditions for judgment is not excused; rather, he is either a sinner or an unbeliever.

If it is required of a judge in matters of the permitted and the forbidden that the means of <term>ijtihad</term> <gloss>independent reasoning</gloss> be gathered in him—which is the knowledge of the <term>usul</term> <gloss>legal fundamentals</gloss> and the knowledge of <term>istinbat</term> <gloss>deduction/inference</gloss> from those fundamentals through <term>qiyas</term> <gloss>analogy</gloss>—how much more so should this be required of the judge who rules on existing things? That is, he must know the <term>awail aqliyya</term> <gloss>rational first principles</gloss> and the method of deduction from them.

In short, error concerning the Law is of two types. First is an error for which a person is excused if they are among those qualified to investigate the subject in which the error occurred. This is similar to how a skilled physician is excused if he makes a mistake in the medical art, or a skilled judge is excused if he errs in a judgment; however, one who is not of that profession is not excused. The second is an error for which no one is excused. If such an error occurs regarding the principles of the Law, it is <term>kufr</term> <gloss>infidelity or unbelief</gloss>, and if it occurs in matters following the principles, it is <term>bid'a</term> <gloss>heretical innovation</gloss>.

This latter type of error concerns things that all classes of demonstration lead to knowing, such that knowledge of that matter is possible for everyone in this way. This includes the acknowledgement of God, Blessed and Exalted be He, the <term>nubuwwat</term> <gloss>prophecies</gloss>, and happiness or misery in the afterlife. This is because these three foundations are reached by the three types of evidence which <note>The three types of evidence refer to the demonstrative, dialectical, and rhetorical methods of reaching truth described earlier in the work.</note>

I met this Sultan outside the city as he was returning from a hunt. I dismounted from my animal for him, so he dismounted from his animal as well and greeted me. He welcomed me warmly. It is a custom among the kings of these lands that if a traveler dismounts for them, they are pleased by his action and increase their hospitality toward him. However, if the traveler greets them while remaining mounted, they find it offensive and displeasing, which often results in the traveler being denied any favors. This happened to me with one of them, and I regretted it. After I greeted him and remounted, he asked about my welfare and my journey. I entered the city with him, and he ordered that I be given the best accommodations. # We have established the distance

from the meridian <note>original: "nisf al-nahar"</note> because the correction <note>original: "al-ta'dil"</note> for the birth of the moon is easier by that method than by working with horizons. The hours of the longest day for the latitude of Jerusalem <note>original: "Bayt al-Maqdis"</note> are fourteen hours and a fraction. The Jewish practice using seasonal hours <note>original: "al-sa'at al-zamaniyya"</note> would not be correct unless the conjunction <note>original: "al- اجتماع", the New Moon</note> for the beginning of <term>Tishrei</term> <gloss>the first month of the Jewish civil year</gloss> occurred exactly with the autumnal equinox <note>original: "al-i'tidal al-kharifi"</note>. However, it never occurs exactly with it; rather, it precedes or follows it by a considerable amount, as we have explained previously.

When we extract the time of the conjunction using the calculation provided by the Jews in the table we analyzed according to their opinion, we proceed from that to the knowledge of the start of the year and the determination of its quality—whether it is deficient, regular, or complete. We already possess the knowledge of whether the year is an ordinary <note>original: "basita"</note> or a leap year <note>original: "kabisa"</note>. We then look in the Table of Limits <note>original: "jadwal al-hudud"</note> for a duration of the days of the week whose two boundaries encompass the time we calculated for the conjunction. We look on the leap year side if it is a leap year, and on the ordinary year side if it is an ordinary year. When we find it, we find next to it the first day of the week for the year and its quality. Once we know the start of the year and its quality, and we combine that quality with its status as ordinary or leap, we can determine from that the passing of the start of the following year.
