"Moving" refers to the external <term>mudra</term> <gloss>consort or ritual gesture</gloss> and the meditative absorption of union. This very essence also exists pervading all of these. The phrase "having a magical form" refers to being like various emanations.

If one asks, "By what method is this accomplished?", the text says "of the circle of the mandala," and so forth. By the word "and so forth," it includes the oral instructions on the two seals <note>likely referring to the karmamudra and jnanamudra</note> and the devotion to the solitary hero practice, among others. Alternatively, by the term "circle of the mandala," one should understand the oral instructions of the <term>Mahamudra</term> <gloss>Great Seal</gloss>.

"Having requested forgiveness" means saying "please forgive me," and "requested" means the act of asking. Because it is filled by all the Buddhas, it is a "city." The word "what" carries the meaning of "for what reason." "Having become deluded" carries the meaning of "I have become possessed by doubt."

In the phrase "mandala" and so forth, "manda" <note>translated from the Tibetan "dkyil"</note> is a synonym for "essence" or "heart." If one asks, "What is that essence?", the text says: "The <term>bodhicitta</term> <gloss>awakened mind</gloss> is great bliss." This is characterized by being free from the suffering produced by all afflictions and secondary afflictions without exception. "Taking that" means making it one's own. "By that" refers to the primordial wisdom of great bliss. "Assembly" <note>original: "’dus pa"</note> is the union with all the Buddhas; this is the meaning of the so-called ultimate mandala. "Like a wheel" is characterized by great bliss. "Abiding" is great compassion. The "space element" is the emptiness of all phenomena. The phrase "purifying the objects and so forth" refers to the character of clear light in which they have become of one taste. Vajra is <unclear>one line of text follows</unclear>

This is the meaning of the phrase "is taught." To teach the names of the <term>chakras</term> <gloss>energy centers or wheels</gloss>, the text mentions "dharma," "enjoyment," and so forth. The term <term>birthplace</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: janmasthana</gloss> refers to the region below the navel. The phrase "three bodies" <note>the trikaya: dharmakaya, sambhogakaya, and nirmanakaya</note> refers to the meaning of complete knowledge.

To demonstrate the logic of the locations associated with the positions of the body, the text says "without exception" and so forth. The word "where" refers to the birthplace <note>the navel or secret chakra</note>. The "subject matter" refers to that which is to be thoroughly taught. The word "there" refers to transformation. Because there is a shared quality of performing emanation, it is called "emanation" <note>the <term>Nirmanakaya</term> or Emanation Body</note>. Furthermore, since the Buddhas reside in the form of the Emanation Body for as long as <term>samsara</term> <gloss>the cycle of existence</gloss> lasts, its location is stable. Therefore, because of this shared quality of being stable, the birthplace is also called the "stable location." For this reason, it is said: "by what and for what reason it is produced."

The term "dharma" refers to the principle that all phenomena are mind-only. Therefore, the location of the <term>Dharmakaya</term> <gloss>Truth Body or Reality Body</gloss> is the mind <note>at the heart center</note>, because that is its dwelling place. Regarding the phrase "certainly enjoying food," "food" refers to that which is consumed or experienced. The term "tastes" should be connected with the word "at the throat." Because the experience of enjoyment is similar, it is called the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>Complete Enjoyment Body</gloss>. If one asks what the Enjoyment Body is, it is the teaching of the secret dharma to the <term>bodhisattvas</term> <gloss>awakening beings</gloss>.

"Great Bliss" refers to the Body of Great Bliss <note>the <term>Mahasukhakaya</term></note>. The phrase "at the crown" refers to residing at the head. In the same way that the four <term>chakras</term> encompass the bodies, they also encompass the "fruits" <gloss>results of practice</gloss> and the "classes" <gloss>divisions</gloss>. To establish this, the text says "E-Vam" and so forth. The "aspect of E-Vam" refers to the <term>chakra</term> of the birthplace.

If one asks what exists there, the text mentions the "causal concordance," which is the fruit. The <term>Dharma Chakra</term> <note>at the heart</note> is the fruit of maturation. The <term>Enjoyment Chakra</term> <note>at the throat</note> is the fruit of human effort. The <term>Chakra of Great Bliss</term> <note>at the crown</note> refers to the meaning of the stainless fruit. If one asks who—

The second point is whether this essence, or even something superior to it called Body, Speech, and Mind, belongs to another. The third point asks, "What is the name of this venerable one?" In order to clarify these conceptions, the text says: "How wonderful!" <note>original: "E ma ho"</note> and so forth. At the end of this phrase, one should take the word "this" from the previous sentence and apply it to understand its own meaning; "this too" means "even one such as this." If the word "this" is absent in some versions, it should still be understood as being present in meaning.

"How wonderful, Vajra Essence!" <note>original: "Vajra-garbha"</note> means that all Bodhisattvas are the <term>Tathagatagarbha</term> <gloss>Essence of the One Gone to Bliss</gloss> and belong to the <term>Tathagata-gotra</term> <gloss>Buddha Family</gloss>. Ignorance, hatred, pride, desire, and jealousy are the five Buddha families. Among these, that which is characterized by hatred is the Vajra Essence. This Bodhisattva's name is consistent with his meaning. It is difficult to find a family of Bodhisattvas such as this. Feeling amazement at that very fact, he calls out, "How wonderful!"

Regarding the phrase, "That Essence, Bodhisattva, Great Hero <note>original: "Mahasattva"</note>, excellent, excellent," the very intention to accomplish the welfare of others through methods such as supreme wrath is Great Compassion. Through that, the awakening that accomplishes various purposes at indefinite times is Great Awakening. One who possesses such pure thought is a "Great Heroic Bodhisattva." One who possesses such an intention to benefit others and an intention to benefit themselves is the supreme of beings. For that reason, the word "excellent" is repeated twice.

"Listen!" is an exhortation to pay attention. This shows that a holy person with such a lineage and such an intention is a fortunate one in this context. If one asks how this family is to be recognized, it is through the specific signs of faith and desire for its qualities. As it says in the *Noble Descent into Lanka Sutra* <note>original: "Arya-Lankavatara-sutra"</note>:

By smoke, one knows there is fire;
By the water-crane, one knows there is water.

This describes the practice. Being filled by that very thing refers to the satisfaction of the Bodhisattvas in each individual moment. Because it never perishes, it arises as a continuous flow and is said to arise constantly, meaning it is eternal. Imperishability refers to the uninterrupted continuity of its constant arising.

In that way, within the utterly pure Buddha fields, one is firmly sustained by the joy and bliss of the taste of the Great Dharma. This is not like sentient beings who are sustained by coarse food and such things. If one asks what it is that satisfies through the taste of Great Wisdom, it is the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>Enjoyment Body</gloss> of the Buddhas. Regarding the statement that this body is called the Great Being <note>original: "Mahasattva"</note>, it is indeed named the Great Being. How so? Because it abides and remains, staying without perishing, it is a Being <note>Sanskrit: Sattva</note>. Because it is both a Being and Great, it is a Great Being, meaning it is utterly imperishable.

Regarding the phrase "always" and so forth: here, the word <term>Samaya</term> <gloss>Pledge/Bond</gloss> should be understood as the Great <term>Samaya</term>. A single word is used to represent the whole category, just as mentioning a terrifying one <note>Yamantaka</note> allows one to understand the entire class of terrifying deities. Through the application of radiating energy, it pervades everywhere, and thus it is the <term>Samaya</term>. Approaching according to the various dispositions of those to be trained through various means is the Great <term>Samaya</term>. A being characterized by the Great <term>Samaya</term> is a Great <term>Samaya</term> Being <note>Mahasamayasattva</note>. "Being" refers to its constant engagement. This is explained through an etymological derivation by extracting the "sa" from <term>satata</term> <gloss>always</gloss> and the "va" from <term>pravritti</term> <gloss>engagement/activity</gloss> and discarding the remainder.

For this reason, it is said: "it is constant engagement." That which is the <term>Nirmanakaya</term> <gloss>Emanation Body</gloss> of the Buddhas, through its infinite divisions, is eternal in its continuity, and therefore it is called "Eternal." This is expressed by the term Great <term>Samaya</term>. For example, when a fire burns in a great wilderness, in some places it spreads, in some it blazes, and in some it dies out. In the same way, the <term>Nirmanakayas</term> of the Buddhas manifest taking birth in other Buddha fields. Having taken birth, they manifest passing into <term>Nirvana</term> <gloss>the state beyond suffering</gloss> in other locations. Thus, in all world realms, they are never absent.

The path which serves as the remedy for all obscurations will arise through the <term>paramitas</term> <gloss>perfections</gloss>. By means of this remedy, the latencies of the <term>dharmas</term> <gloss>phenomena</gloss> associated with the afflictions accumulated in the <term>alayavijnana</term> <gloss>storehouse consciousness</gloss> are completely exhausted. The consciousnesses appearing as the environment, the body, and enjoyments then cease. Having abandoned the characteristics of the storehouse consciousness, one fully adopts the characteristics of the stainless realm. This very stainless realm is the <term>kaya</term> <gloss>body</gloss> of the Buddhas. Based upon that attainment, one achieves the <term>sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>complete enjoyment body</gloss> and the <term>nirmanakaya</term> <gloss>emanation body</gloss>. This is the established philosophical position. 

According to this tenet, the Perfection of Wisdom itself should be meditated upon for the sake of Buddhahood. This is because, through the division of two types of meaning, there is the primordial wisdom of the authentic absence of entities, which is certain in its non-duality. By this, the various <unclear>false</unclear> appearances of duality subside, and an infinite, clear luminosity appears.

If one then thinks: "The meditation on the forms of <term>Heruka</term> <gloss>a semi-wrathful male deity</gloss> and the <term>yoginis</term> <gloss>female tantric deities</gloss>, as well as on mantras, signs, seats, and celestial palaces, involves mental proliferation and is erroneous; it gives rise to the cyclic existence of afflictions and is not the cause of liberation." 

To clarify this, it is said: "Liberation is achieved through the very nature of entities." Here, "entities" refers to that which establishes a firm abiding and is intended to mean the thorough attainment of all the qualities of a Buddha. Those possessing great compassion are liberated through the six perfections themselves; for that very reason, they are addressed as "Great Compassionate Ones." 

Being liberated by the Perfection of Wisdom alone quickly abandons the afflictions and results in the state of an <term>Arhat</term> <gloss>one who has overcome internal enemies</gloss>. Therefore, one proceeds predominantly toward the enlightenment of a <term>Sravaka</term> <gloss>pious listener</gloss> and not toward the enlightenment of a Buddha. The <term>Bodhisattva</term> <gloss>hero of enlightenment</gloss> who possesses great compassion supremeley accomplishes the benefit of sentient beings and aspires toward unsurpassed enlightenment, not toward the lower paths. Such a one is liberated by the six perfections together, not by one alone. If one is liberated by the six, what then is the function of the first five, and what does the sixth perform?

Is it not so? This means that for which there is <term>falsity</term> <gloss>original: brdzun pa/rdzun pa</gloss>. The great elements and so forth are imputed by a mistaken consciousness. Their individual essence does not exist. Therefore, they dissolve into non-mistaken <term>gnosis</term> <gloss>original: ye shes</gloss>. It is excellent if the <term>Madhyamaka</term> <gloss>Middle Way School</gloss> and the <term>Yogacara</term> <gloss>Yoga Practice School</gloss> agree on this tenet: everything does not exist in a dualistic manner, and everything is not non-existent in the manner of mere clarity that is non-dual. Other positions, such as the three Madhyamaka and the four Yogacara views, have been refuted by those skilled in valid cognition, scripture, and treatises.

Furthermore, if one asks how this great gnosis is <term>Hevajra</term> <gloss>the Tantric deity "Diamond Joy"</gloss>, it is the nature of great wisdom and great compassion. From what does this arise? It is the nature of accomplishing the welfare of all beings for all time, and the nature of what is to be attained by meditating on the qualities of the Buddhas and the qualities of the Bodhisattvas. This is because it is the very vessel for those qualities.

If that is so, then while that is the <term>Causal Tantra</term> <gloss>original: rgyu'i rgyud</gloss>, how is it the <term>Method Tantra</term> <gloss>original: thabs kyi rgyud</gloss>? This is true: it is the very thing that blesses the body, the all-pervading nature, the mere clarity, the illuminating nature, the great bliss, the vessel for the qualities of the Buddhas, and the condensation of all Great Vehicle teachings. If one constantly keeps this in mind, all the <term>Tathagatas</term> <gloss>Thus-Gone Ones</gloss> will grant their blessing. Because the primary Method Tantra here is the appearance of the one who meditates and the object of meditation as inseparable, it is indeed the Method Tantra.

For the purpose of meditating on this great gnosis, the blessing of all is performed through its <term>mudra</term> <gloss>symbolic hand gesture or consort</gloss> as follows: it is the subtle syllable <term>Hum</term> without remainder, with vowels, the moon, and the <term>bindu</term> <gloss>drop or point</gloss>, yet without a bindu; a subtlety the size of a mustard seed; or extremely subtle; or the placement of the four syllables according to the divisions of the four <term>chakras</term> <gloss>energy centers</gloss>.

If one asks whether this aspect of the mudra belongs to the <term>Generation Stage</term> <gloss>original: bskyed rim</gloss> and not the <term>Completion Stage</term> <gloss>original: rdzogs rim</gloss>, that is not the case. The term "Generation Stage" here is used according to worldly convention.

Thus, there are sixteen shifts in a full day and night cycle. The mention of sixty-four sticks <note>original: "དབྱུ་གུ་", refers to a specific unit of time measurement often translated as a "cane" or "staff" length of time</note> pertains to the full day and night. Two sticks constitute one water-clock unit <note>original: "ཆུ་ཚོད་", a measure of roughly 24 minutes</note>. There are thirty-two water-clock units in a day and night. A quarter of a session is a water-clock unit. Four sessions constitute either a day or a night, meaning there are eight sessions in a full twenty-four-hour period. To this point, the verse says:

Upon that, one should visualize the garland of thirty-four consonants starting with <term>Ka</term> <gloss>the Sanskrit alphabet consonants</gloss> in the same manner, transforming into the disk of a sun. This transformation of the <term>Kali</term> <gloss>consonant garland</gloss> into the sun is the Sun of <term>Kali</term>; it is the Wisdom of Equality. The phrase "The seed-syllable is placed in the center" means it resides in the very center of the sun. On top of the center of the sun, the blue <term>vajra</term> <gloss>scepter or diamond-bolt</gloss> born from the seed-syllable resides there. This is the meaning of the statement, "The seed-syllable resides in the center of the navel." This very mind that has transformed into the form of the seed-syllable <term>Hum</term> is called the "Being" <note>referring to the Sattva in Vajrasattva</note>. This refers to the one born as the seed-syllable being called <term>Vajrasattva</term> <gloss>Vajra Being</gloss>.

What is its nature? It has the nature of supreme bliss, which is the nature of method and wisdom. From the union of the <term>Ali</term> <gloss>vowels</gloss> as the moon and the <term>Kali</term> <gloss>consonants</gloss> as the sun, there are three stages of the nature of great bliss: the union, the actual manifestation, and the conclusion. This is the Wisdom of Discernment. Regarding the term "emanating forth," this occurs from that very seed-syllable of one's own. As for "what is emanated," it is "an image of one's own body," such as the body of <term>Hevajra</term>. This includes all the deities of the mantra in summary: blue in color, possessing a wrathful expression, and appearing in the forms of the fifteen <term>yoginis</term> <gloss>female tantric deities</gloss>. These serve as the method to subdue all sentient beings, adorning and filling the sphere of space. The phrase "should be reabsorbed into the heart" means that all those forms of the deities are reabsorbed and dissolved back into that very seed-syllable. The unification of all these into one's own mantra seed-syllable is the All-Accomplishing Wisdom.

Then, "The practitioner becomes the nature of hatred" <note>referring to the transmutation of the 'hatred' emotion associated with the Akshobhya Buddha family</note> means that through the complete transformation of the moon, sun, vajra, and seed-syllable, the body of Hevajra arises. Possessing the colors, ornaments, expressions, and attributes that will be described, these constitute the Wisdom of the Dharmadhatu <gloss>Sphere of Reality</gloss> which is utterly pure. This is the attainment of great enlightenment in the essence of the sublime transformation of the basis. Thus, the awakening through the five wisdoms, such as the Mirror-like Wisdom and so on, is the Awakening in Five Aspects. This will be explained in the eighth chapter: the moon possesses Mirror-like Wisdom, and the "Seven-Horsed One" <note>an epithet for the Sun</note> is Equality. Through the deity's own—

The seed syllables and hand symbols are explained as discriminating awareness. One should diligently strive for the unification of all things. This is the ultimate purity of the <term>dharmadhatu</term> <gloss>the realm of phenomena or absolute reality</gloss>. The wise have taught that these five aspects are to be meditated upon.

Regarding the statement, "he becomes the embodiment of hatred," hatred here refers to <term>Hevajra</term> <gloss>the Joyful Vajra</gloss>. If one asks what he is like: his color appears blue and red. The phrase "or <term>Mahakala</term>" <gloss>the Great Black One</gloss> completes the description. The phrase "red <term>bandhu</term>" refers to his red eyes; thus, he is "the one with eyes like the red <term>bandhujivaka</term> flower." The phrase "a mass of orange hair bristling upward" refers to his hair being orange and standing on end. 

"With the five <term>mudras</term>" refers to the ornaments of the symbolic seals. "The skull marked by a <term>vajra</term>" refers to a <term>vajra</term>-skull. "He holds it" is added to complete the sentence. "Possessing the nature of expression" refers to the manner of expression. These three points demonstrate the application of the solitary hero.

The following is taught concerning the fourth yoga. Regarding the phrase "the charnel ground" and so forth, there are five stages of yoga: <term>shamatha</term> <gloss>calm abiding</gloss>, <term>vipashyana</term> <gloss>special insight</gloss>, the cultivation of both together, and the great joy in both, which is the view. The <term>mudra</term> <gloss>seal or gesture</gloss> of this joy is the play that prevents distraction. Therefore, it is called "play." 

"The eight" refers to <term>Gauri</term> and the other goddesses. Just as with the branches of the third yoga, so it is with the fourth. As for the body of yoga, one should visualize the eight charnel grounds and so forth in the cardinal and intermediate directions within the four walls. In their center, one should meditate on the two stages of the mandala of the residence, which will be explained. In the center of that, just as the three types of meditative absorption of the sixteen-armed Shri Heruka will be explained, one should likewise meditate on the two-armed form. 

Here, the union of the Blessed One surrounded by the eight <term>yoginis</term> constitutes the fourth yoga, and it is not the solitary hero practice. If one asks why he plays in the charnel grounds, the text says "charnel ground" and so forth. By showing one word, it applies to other words. For example, by saying "the Terrifier," one understands the class of terrifiers; if one says "not," it implies "immortal" <note>original: "amrita"</note>; if one says "U," it implies "Umapati" <gloss>Lord of Uma</gloss>.

I am also the worldly beings. Just as I am the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>Complete Enjoyment Body</gloss>, which is the natural result of the <term>Dharmakaya</term> <gloss>Truth Body</gloss> of Great Bliss, I am also the world that has become the natural result of the Great Bliss of the father, the mother, and the beings of the <term>bardo</term> <gloss>intermediate state</gloss>. I am also the beings of the <term>gandharva</term> <gloss>scent-eater</gloss> realm who are swooning with Great Bliss. 

If one asks how that which is the Great Bliss of worldly beings is the primary object of meditation, it is said: "That which is called Sahajānanda" <note>original: "lhan cig skyes dga'", meaning Co-emergent Joy</note> and so forth. 

Furthermore, if it is asked: "Since you are the primary Great Bliss to be accomplished, and the co-emergent joy of cyclic existence is not the thing to be accomplished, why are you the primary object of accomplishment?" It is said: "If that is so, then I..." and so forth. 

The word "also" functions here as a causal term, because it creates confidence in that very thing as the primary focus. Because the realization is established through a corresponding example, that very thing is designated as "I, the primary one." 

"Like a lamp in the darkness" means that just as a lamp clarifies and allows one to perceive a vase or other objects in a dark room, the <term>Sahajānanda</term> <gloss>Co-emergent Joy</gloss> of the example clarifies the bliss that is to be accomplished.

Just as it is said that the sky becomes clear in its pure state, so too is this emptiness. In its impure state, because it is not distinct from the ordinary world of childish beings <note>refers to spiritually immature individuals or non-Aryas</note>, it is expressed through terms such as form. However, in its pure state, it is called emptiness. Therefore, the essential meaning is that there are no phenomena, such as form, that exist separately from emptiness.

Thus, since there is no distinction between phenomena <term>dharma</term> <gloss>things or events</gloss> and the nature of phenomena <term>dharmata</term> <gloss>the intrinsic reality or suchness of things</gloss>, whenever the nature of phenomena is used to describe a phenomenon, form itself is called emptiness. Whenever a phenomenon is used to describe the nature of phenomena, emptiness is also called form. 

Furthermore, regarding the statement that form itself is emptiness and emptiness is form: emptiness is suchness, and it refers to the form that is the nature of phenomena. Because those forms that are imagined <term>parikalpita</term> <gloss>the mentally constructed nature</gloss> and conceptually analyzed <term>vikalpita</term> <gloss>the dependent nature under conceptual dualism</gloss> do not exist at all, and because it is improper to dwell even upon the perfected form <term>parinispanna</term> <gloss>the thoroughly established nature of reality</gloss>, it is said: one should not dwell on form. The same should be applied to feeling and the other aggregates.

The phrase one should not dwell on the letters means one should not dwell on the individual syllables of the alphabet, such as A and so forth.

The phrase one should not dwell on the realization of the letters refers to the following: the knowledge of <term>dharani</term> <gloss>incantations or mnemonic formulas</gloss> which arises by relying on the syllables such as A and follows the meaning of non-arising. This is called the realization of the letters. It is taught that one should not dwell even on that. 

Because that knowledge of <term>dharani</term> is itself unborn from the beginning, it is realized through the expression: A is the door to all phenomena. Some Bodhisattvas with the sharpest faculties may achieve perfect enlightenment by relying on this single meaning of non-arising. Those with middling faculties rely on two letters, and through familiarizing themselves with those two expressions, they proceed.

As for the "Door of Retention" <note>original: <term>dharani-mukha</term></note> of the Great Vehicle, what are these doors of retention? They are: the equality of the nature of syllables, the door of syllables, and the entrance into syllables. Regarding "retention," there are four types mentioned in the description of the qualities of a Bodhisattva: the retention of patience, the retention of the teachings, the retention of meaning, and the retention of mantras. The doors to these are the "doors of retention," which are the syllables themselves. Through the power of definitive contemplation on these syllables, these four retentions will arise. What is the nature of those syllables? The nature of syllables is the thorough realization of the ultimate meaning. The equality of the nature of syllables is the sameness of the nature of syllables, such as the syllable "A" <note>in Buddhist linguistics, the letter "A" represents the unborn or unoriginated nature of all phenomena</note>.

It does not abide for the sake of expanding the phenomena of the directions. It is said that it is not for the sake of decreasing, nor is it for the sake of increasing. The statement "the Perfection of Wisdom does not abide in duality" means that if it were to abide in the manner of grasping and not grasping and so forth, then it would exist in the nature of duality and the nature of distinctness. Similarly, generosity, ethical discipline, and the other perfections are also of a single essence in the ultimate state. Because they lack distinction, they are non-dual. For this reason, it is taught: "Kaushika, to think of suchness as dual is merely a misconception." All of these, such as the Perfection of Wisdom and the rest, are one within the nature of <term>tathata</term> <gloss>suchness</gloss> and abide without duality.

Regarding the statement, "I do not perceive any phenomenon that attains complete and perfect enlightenment, nor any phenomenon by which one attains it," the meaning is as follows: By means of the wisdom of knowing all aspects, which encompasses conventional knowledge, one knows all phenomena in every possible aspect. However, when analyzed by ultimate wisdom, like the objects seen in a dream, one does not see any agent who knows or any phenomenon to be known. 

Regarding the statement, "O sons of the gods, it is because all phenomena are utterly pure," here, "purity" refers to the very absence of any entity. This is a synonym for saying they are "utterly non-existent."

Regarding the statement, "O Blessed One, it is not difficult to attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment," this is because all phenomena are non-existent. It is not difficult to realize that a non-entity is indeed a non-entity. What is difficult is to realize the true nature of things if they were existent phenomena. It is not difficult to know and accomplish the realization that what is non-existent is merely a non-entity. If phenomena truly existed, one would need to accomplish practices such as the <term>paramitas</term> <gloss>perfections</gloss> in order to increase virtuous qualities and abandon non-virtuous ones. However, because these phenomena do not exist, the accomplishment is not difficult. Therefore, it is said that "it is not difficult to attain complete and perfect enlightenment."

Regarding the Elder <term>Shariputra</term>'s <gloss>one of the Buddha's primary disciples, known for his wisdom</gloss> statement that enlightenment is difficult to attain, his intended meaning was this: All phenomena are in essence non-entities; once one realizes they are non-entities like space, if it were enough to simply remain in silence, then it would not be difficult. However, while one must realize that in truth there is no complete and perfect enlightenment of any phenomenon, one must subsequently still engage in the practices of the <term>paramitas</term> <gloss>perfections</gloss> and also [attain] all phenomena completely and perfectly.

Regarding the question, "What are the four total purities?": 
1. The total purity of the foundation is when all the bad tendencies of the afflictions of all sentient beings are completely separated from their foundations, and one attains mastery over taking up one's own body as desired, as well as over staying and transferring <note>dying and reincarnating</note>.
2. The total purity of the object is when one attains mastery over all objects of focus, including those categorized as emanations and transformations.
3. The total purity of the mind is the increase of virtue in the mind in every possible way through being separated from all bad tendencies of the mind.
4. The total purity of primordial wisdom <term>jnana</term> <gloss>exalted knowledge</gloss> is the mastery of unimpeded knowledge regarding all that is to be known, through being separated from all bad tendencies on the side of ignorance.

Regarding the question, "What are the ten masteries?":

# The Explanation of the Noble Fourfold Dharma

Homage to Manjushri, the youthful.

Why was this <term>sutra</term> <gloss>discourse</gloss> composed, which states: "A <term>bodhisattva mahasattva</term> <gloss>great heroic being for enlightenment</gloss> should not abandon these four dharmas for the duration of their life, even for the sake of their own life"?

It was composed to correctly teach those who are confused about the methods for attaining unsurpassed enlightenment after having entered the Great Vehicle <note>Mahayana</note>. It was also composed to cause the heedless to correctly take up the practice, to encourage those who are discouraged, and to bring joy to those who have correctly entered the path.

The number four is mentioned specifically to prevent people from losing interest or being overwhelmed by an excessive amount of information. By stating a number, the teachings are easily remembered. Furthermore, although patience and gentleness are mentioned later, they share a single purpose and are thus not fundamentally different.

Although there are many terms for those who have correctly entered the Great Vehicle, two names <note>Bodhisattva and Mahasattva</note> are used for three reasons: because of their aspiration, their application, and their realization.

How is it through aspiration? They are called a <term>bodhisattva</term> because they aspire toward the profound objects of knowledge. They are called a <term>mahasattva</term> because they aspire toward great power.

How is it through application? Because they exert themselves for the sake of their own unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and for the sake of completely protecting all sentient beings from suffering.

How is it through realization? Because enlightenment is realized through two strengths. What are the two? They are the strength of intelligence and the strength of diligence. One cannot realize enlightenment through ignorance or through minor diligence.

<margin>Poison even in the best things.</margin>
Who is there who would dare to deny that poison lies hidden and exists even in the best of things? All are compelled to confess this. If this is true, I now ask of you whether the poison should not be separated from what is good and useful? And the good taken, and the evil left behind? Indeed, it must be so. If therefore it must be so, I ask you to explain to me how it is separated in your workshops? For among you, all things remain mixed together. Yet, so that you may protect your own simplicity, if you are forced to confess that poison lies hidden there and are asked where it finally goes, you then bring forth some nonsense about "corrections" which supposedly demand and carry away the poison.
<margin>The correction of the Physicians is discussed.</margin>
Just as they say Quinces correct Scammony, and then <term>Diagridium</term> <gloss>a preparation of Scammony juice</gloss>. But what kind of correction is that? Does the poison not remain afterward just as it was at first? And yet you meanwhile boast that you have corrected it, so that the poison no longer harms. But where did it escape to?
<margin>Diagridion.</margin>
It remains in the <term>Diagridium</term>. Test it, if you are wise: exceed the proper measure, and you will see where the poison is. For you will know it quite quickly. Thus you also correct <term>Turbith</term> <gloss>an ayurvedic purgative root</gloss>, and you call it <term>Diaturbith</term>. Such are your "corrections," which would be suitable for peasants and should be given to pack-horses. Make a trial by exceeding the measure and increase the dose; you will see whether you do not feel the poison.
<margin>What it is to correct a Medicine.</margin>
*To correct is to take what has been corrected.* If one who is malicious and has sinned is punished, the correction does not extend further than the will of the one who was punished lasts. Such are these corrections of yours also; the matter rests with the things themselves, not with you. Now, in this case, a Physician must consider nothing further than that the poison be removed. This must be done through separation. As, for example: a serpent is poisonous, and yet it is adopted as food. If you remove the poison from it, you may eat it with no harm. The same must be understood equally concerning all other things, namely, that a similar separation is necessary. Until that is done, you cannot be secure in your operation, unless by chance it happens that nature supplies your lack, or a greater kindness of the heavens favors you. For in your art, no protection remains.

Now, therefore, let that true foundation be established, if it must be, which removes the poison, just as Alchemy provides. For this must be done in such a way that if Mars <note>the metal iron or the martial quality</note> is in the Sun <note>the metal gold or the solar quality</note>, Mars is removed; and if Saturn <note>the metal lead</note> dwells in Venus <note>the metal copper</note>, it is separated from her. For as many ascendants and impressions as there are in the things of nature, so many bodies exist within them. Truly, those bodies which are contrary must have something entirely removed and taken away, so that in this way all contrariety is abolished, and the evil is taken from the good which you seek.
<margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin>
As gold is useful for nothing unless it is first cast into the fire, so Medicine is much less useful if it does not pass through the fire. For it is necessary for all things to pass through the fire into another generation, by which it ought to benefit and help man. And should this not rightly be considered the honest foundation of any Physician? For a Physician ought not to apply poisons, but rather <term>arcana</term>.
<margin>The workshops are rebuked.</margin>
However, all those workshop preparations, as many as there are, do not contribute even a tiny letter to this doctrine. Instead, they are simply occupied in "correcting." It is as if a dog farted in a room, and that stench were suppressed either by lozenges and incense, or by juniper wood. I ask you, does the stench not remain in the room afterward just as much as before? And although it is indeed not perceived by the sense of smell, is it therefore permitted for anyone to say the stench has been separated and no longer remains? On the contrary, it is present, but corrected by the perfume. Thus, the perfume and the foul air enter the nostrils together.
